question: A 35-year-old woman with Graves' hyperthyroidism presents to the eye clinic. On examination she has bilateral lid retraction with visible sclera above the limbus (Dalrymple's sign) and lid lag on downgaze (von Graefe's sign). The MOST likely mechanism of lid retraction in thyroid eye disease is:

answers.text: Spasm of the orbicularis oculi muscle due to sympathetic overactivity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Orbicularis oculi is a lid-closing muscle innervated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). Its spasm causes blepharospasm (involuntary lid closure), not lid retraction. Thyroid eye disease primarily affects the lid ELEVATORS and orbital fibroblasts.

answers.text: Fibrosis and shortening of Müller's muscle and the levator complex with sympathetic overstimulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Lid retraction in thyroid eye disease results from: (1) sympathetic overstimulation of Müller's muscle (the sympathetically innervated superior tarsal muscle), causing upper lid retraction; (2) over-action and eventual fibrosis of the levator–Müller complex secondary to glycosaminoglycan infiltration of orbital fibroblasts. Lower lid retraction occurs from fibrosis of the inferior rectus and its fascial attachments. Both components explain the 'staring' appearance.

answers.text: Proptosis pushing the globe forward and mechanically stretching the upper lid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While proptosis does contribute to the 'staring' appearance, lid retraction in thyroid eye disease is primarily due to intrinsic changes in the levator–Müller complex and sympathetic overstimulation, not simply mechanical globe protrusion. These are distinct and independently present pathologies.

answers.text: Third cranial nerve palsy causing aberrant regeneration to the levator

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aberrant regeneration of CN III can cause 'pseudo-lid retraction' (e.g. lid elevates on adduction — Marcus Gunn jaw-winking equivalent), but this is not the mechanism in thyroid eye disease. CN III palsy itself causes ptosis, not retraction.

overallFeedback.feedback: Lid retraction in thyroid eye disease = sympathetic overactivity of Müller's muscle + levator/conjunctival fibrosis from glycosaminoglycan infiltration. Dalrymple's sign (scleral show above limbus) + von Graefe's sign (lid lag on downgaze) together are the hallmark. Proptosis and lid retraction co-exist but are mechanistically distinct.

Well done. Remember the mnemonic for Dalrymple + von Graefe + Kocher: lid retraction = sympathetic overactivity (Müller's) + levator fibrosis. This triad is pathognomonic for thyroid eye disease (Parsons' 23rd ed).
